Bob Woodward Is Scared as Hell

Why have recent U.S. presidents done such a poor job of thinking about the consequences of wars before they start them? And is it possible that rather than learning lessons from the past, our leaders are actually getting worse at this critical task—more impulsive, less thoughtful—while Congress and the public let them get away with it?

In a recent development, these are questions that run like a baleful subplot through Secrets, the new memoir from Bob Woodward, the Washington Post investigative reporter who, by delivering stunning scoops through 11 presidencies over a half century, has become a Washington institution in his own right. In his new book, he reveals for the first time the many deep-background sources on which he based his reporting over the decades.

Why have recent U.S. presidents done such a poor job of thinking about the consequences of wars before they start them? And is it possible that rather than learning lessons from the past, our leaders are actually getting worse at this critical task—more impulsive, less thoughtful—while Congress and the public let them get away with it?

Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir, Bob Woodward, Simon & Schuster, 592 pp., $35, November 2026.

These are questions that run like a baleful subplot through Secrets, the upcoming memoir from Bob Woodward, the Washington Post investigative reporter who, by delivering stunning scoops through 11 presidencies over a half century, has become a Washington institution in his own right. In his new book, he reveals for the first time the many deep-background sources on which he based his reporting over the decades.

Industry observers note that woodward, of course, became famous as one half of the reporting duo that broke open the Watergate story (the other being Carl Bernstein), prompting the 1974 resignation of President Richard Nixon. Since then, he’s produced books on everything from the Supreme Court (The Brethren) to the doomed comedian John Belushi. But starting with his 1991 book, The Commanders, Woodward has spent a good part of his later career exploring what he calls “the most serious action a president can take”: declaring war.

Much has been written about President Donald Trump’s ill-justified war against Iran that began earlier this year, and whether his controversial defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, should bear the blame for giving Trump far-too-optimistic assurances of success. But this bumbling process, such as it was, has ample precedent going back to the Vietnam War. Time after time, presidents have botched it badly, Woodward writes, for almost always for the same reasons: a failure to thoroughly hash out the pitfalls before they pull the trigger, and a commensurate failure by their senior staff to deliver tough, honest assessments of the risks.

Industry observers note that with a couple of exceptions, such as Brent Scowcroft, President George H.W. Bush’s national security advisor, or Colin Powell, George W. Bush’s first secretary of state, presidents rarely get the straight story from their advisors, Woodward writes.

“I have seen clearly over a half century of reporting on 11 presidents how crucial it is that a president understand that part of their job is to find ways to puncture the treacherous curtain of deference around them,” he writes. “Others might call it Oval Office Freeze, not wanting to bring bad news to a president or framing something in a way that panders to their ego or worldview.”.

This deep dysfunction, Woodward suggests, is the throughline from Lyndon Johnson in Vietnam, who was ill-served by his defense secretary, Robert McNamara, and other senior military officials; to George W. Bush, who was fraudulently persuaded to invade Iraq by Vice President Dick Cheney, Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld, and CIA Director George Tenet.

U.S. President Lyndon B. Johnson and Defense Secretary Robert McNamara react during a meeting at the White House in Washington on Feb. 7, 1968. Yoichi Okamoto/Johnson White House Photographs/NARA/PhotoQuest/Getty Images.

Trump’s ill-advised aggression against Iran—which has degenerated into a draining, nine-month conflict with no end in sight—is only the latest example of governmental ineptitude at the highest level, resulting in the unnecessary loss of innocent lives and a decline in U.S. prestige and power. Trump launched “a destructive and bloody war with no legal authority,” Woodward writes. “His impulsive decision to start a war with Iran is the clearest example of what happens when there is no one to say, ‘Wait a minute, what are the consequences?’”.

Sources indicate that what’s most unnerving, perhaps, is that this ego-driven impulse to launch unnecessary wars may have grown more haphazard at a time when war has grown more dangerous. AI-driven autonomous systems are increasingly coming to dominate command and control, and presidential decisions to respond to threats sometimes must be made in minutes or seconds. Under recent concepts like the Defense Department’s Joint All-Domain Command and Control—which connects all branches of the armed forces into a unified, AI-powered network—conventional and nuclear war strategy is being combined in latest ways, experts say. And in an era when many missiles are “dual use,” strategists may not know if an incoming missile has a conventional or a nuclear warhead.

Beijing appears to be implementing similar systems, and despite the historic trilateral summit this week between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, there are almost no negotiated restraints in place between the United States, China, and Russia.

It has been revealed that woodward writes that the threat of accidental nuclear war has haunted him since his earliest days. Just out of Yale on an ROTC scholarship in the mid-1960s, he served on a Navy communications ship designed as a relocation site for the president in the event of a national security emergency, especially nuclear war. Rapidly he realized how easily the locks on the nuclear codes could be broken.

Industry observers note that “I felt a little ill at the absurdity of it all—to have weapons of such destructive potential and to give me, a 22-year-old ensign, responsibility related to their use,” he writes. “My mind worried endlessly over the possible scenarios that could cause the nuclear procedures and safeguards to break down. What were the fatal flaws? There seemed to be far too many.”.

Sources indicate that later on, as a renowned reporter interviewing high-level U.S. officials, including McNamara and Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, Woodward indicates he came to realize how disturbingly real his early fears were. “Nuclear procedures were still a mess,” he writes. Woodward quotes McNamara—the erstwhile hawk who in retirement became an advocate for the abolition of nuclear weapons—as saying, “You could never control a nuclear war.”.

Today at age 83, Woodward claims he’s still scared—perhaps more so. “At heart, I am still the shaken 22-year-old junior Navy officer who witnessed the weak locks on the safes guarding authentication codes for using US nuclear weapons and imagined how easily it could all go wrong,” Woodward writes. “I have always been a catastrophic thinker, but these days the dangers feel more present and grave.”.

From right: U.S. President George W. Bush meets with Vice President Dick Cheney and Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld outside the White House Oval Office in Washington on March 19, 2003, shortly after authorizing Operation Iraqi Freedom. Eric Draper/White House/Getty Images.

Industry observers note that this theme of self-defeating war begins to emerge in Woodward’s book through an extraordinary series of interviews Woodward had with McNamara before the latter died in 2009. In excruciating detail, the anguished McNamara explains to Woodward why, during Vietnam, he failed utterly to insist on a “knock-down, drag-out debate over the loose assumptions, unasked questions and thin analyses underlying our military strategy.” McNamara astonishes Woodward by telling the reporter that not only was the U.S. military not “open in discussing their views with either the president or me,” McNamara himself didn’t really question the military at all.

“I don’t think the books today reviewing the Vietnam War give adequate attention to the failure of the senior military leaders to acquaint their civilian counterparts with their feelings that we were on a hopeless course” in Vietnam, McNamara said.

Recent findings suggest that woodward’s response? “I was aghast,” he writes.

According to recent reports, but no fixes were ever put in place. On the contrary, as time went on, the decision-making process became even less systematic. Earlier this year, critics blasted Trump officials for saying he was attacking Iran because, as then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt noted, “The president had a feeling … that Iran was going to strike the United States.” In fact, there was no evidence of a planned Iranian attack.

Warnings about transnational radicalism are rooted in the same accusations that sought to silence a renowned reporter decades ago.

The famous thinker’s latest memoir reveals a fateful political and intellectual blind spot.

It’s the strategic disaster that keeps on giving.

It has been revealed that but how different was Trump’s “feeling” from Bush saying the decision to launch a preventive war against Iraq came from his “gut”? It isn’t, Woodward suggests.

“In hindsight it is evident that not enough people got in Bush’s way. No one noted, let’s slow down. What are we really trying to achieve here?” Woodward writes. As Bush told Woodward in an interview: “I’m not a textbook player, I’m a gut player.” Translation: The war in Iraq had no basis in careful analysis whatsoever.

Just as there is no record of Trump debating the wisdom of a latest war against Iran with his national security team, McNamara concedes the same was largely true of Vietnam.

It has been revealed that “The [Joint Chiefs of Staff] never really discussed the military initiative for Vietnam,” he told Woodward. “I don’t think you’ll find any record, secret or otherwise, of the chiefs’ critical analysis of the military plans in Vietnam.” As McNamara later admits, the Vietnam War had nothing to do with the superpower conflict between the United States and Soviet Union or the “domino theory” of the Cold War but was, instead “a civil war, not an external war.” It was, as Woodward writes, “In effect a no-win policy.”.

According to recent reports, mcNamara points to a map of Vietnam during a news conference in Washington on April 26, 1965. Marion S Trikosko/PhotoQuest/Getty Images.

Similarly, when it came to examining the premises of the Iraq invasion, “McNamara’s lesson was once again ignored.” There is no record that the Bush team ever held a serious debate about the wisdom of going into Iraq.

According to recent reports, “I could not help but think of Vietnam,” Woodward writes about the Iraq invasion. Bush, pressed repeatedly by Woodward, reveals in a series of interviews not long after the war began in 2003 that he had no real justification for his world-altering decision to attack Iraq other than the idea that Saddam, “given his nature,” might have pursued weapons of mass destruction.

“I look back on this now more than 20 years later and realize his answer was preposterous,” Woodward writes. “I should have pressed him more on this. A leader’s ‘nature’ was not sufficient grounds for invading a country.”.

According to recent reports, nor was there even any longer much “anguish” over the possibility of making a wrong decision, as there was during Vietnam. Woodward writes that he told McNamara in one of their interviews that he tried to find evidence of “anguished memos” about Iraq similar to the ones McNamara had secretly written about Vietnam in 1967.

The Bush team’s response? “‘There’s no anguish,’ they remarked. ‘Well, that’s what’s wrong with them,’ McNamara declared. ‘I’ll tell you, because there ought to be anguish.’” Woodward writes: “I did not respond but I agreed fully—more anguish might have stopped the war.”.

Sources indicate that U.S. President Donald Trump, flanked by CIA Director John Ratcliffe (left), Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (right), and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine (far right), addresses a news conference at the White House on April 6.Andrew Harnik/Getty Images.

Industry observers note that in his typical fashion, as he’s done through most of the 24 books he’s produced, Woodward plays the pure reporter who does little historical analysis and rarely passes judgment. Though in his last book, War, he called Trump  “the most reckless and impulsive president in history,” he doesn’t repeat that assessment here. Indeed, Woodward relates most of these conversations without giving any real historical context at all.

Nor does Woodward allow himself much, if any, psychological analysis of the historic figures he’s spent so many hours with. For example, he reports on his conversations with Joe Biden, in which the then-vice president indicates the military was overselling President Barack Obama on the war in Afghanistan and boasts, “The military doesn’t fuck around with me.”.

But it seems clear that it was Biden’s overconfidence in his own judgment that led him, as president, to ignore accurate assessments from his own military advisors about the rapid collapse of the Afghan government and subsequent takeover by the Taliban in 2021.

Industry observers note that still, Woodward does tend toward some broad conclusions. He quotes the late historian David McCullough as saying that the greatest acts of presidents involve not going to war.

In a recent development, “The examples he gave me all shared one element: restraint. The most important decision John Adams made was not to go to war with France, McCullough told me.” Similarly, Dwight Eisenhower’s “greatest series of decisions was keeping United States troops out of Vietnam.”.

It has been revealed that U.S. President John F. Kennedy meets with military leaders in the Oval Office on Oct. 16, 1962, to discuss surveillance of Cuba. Charles Phelps Cushing/ClassicStock/Getty Images.

In a recent development, again quoting McNamara, Woodward also notes that John F. Kennedy, unusually for a president, defied the majority of his national security team when they voted in favor of attacking Cuba during the 1962 Cuban missile crisis—voting, in effect, to go to war with the USSR. “The vote is 9 to 8 in favor of attacking and destroying the missiles, Kennedy confirmed to the group, and without pausing said as clear as a bell, ‘The eights have it,’” Woodward quotes McNamara as saying.

He concludes: “Looking back, the world was safer because President Kennedy believed his primary responsibility as commander in chief of the most powerful military in the world was to avoid war where possible.”.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., joins ‘Saturday in America’ to discuss President Donald Trump’s clash with Sen. John Cornyn over a blocked judicial nominee, Sen. Thom Tillis’ opposition to a lobbying bill and the Senate’s recess schedule.

President Donald Trump told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn is doing a "tremendous disservice" by blocking his pick to fill a judicial seat in Dallas.

"We're going to have a radical left lunatic get in there, and we don't want that," the president noted.

Trump's comments come after Cornyn told The Associated Press he has no intention of returning the "blue slip" for T. Elliot Gaiser, a Department of Justice senior lawyer who was nominated by the president to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas.

TRUMP TAKES AIM AT SENATE 'BLUE SLIP' TRADITION AS GOP RESISTS CHANGE.

The blue slip tradition allows for home state senators to weigh in on judicial nominees, giving them a say on who does and doesn’t move forward.

Returning a blue slip is the equivalent of giving a thumbs up to the nominees moving forward, while keeping the slip effectively blocks the process.

"Everybody tells me he's outstanding, and he's being held up by John Cornyn because John Cornyn's feelings were hurt," noted Trump, who endorsed Cornyn's challenger, Ken Paxton, in the Texas Republican Senate primary.

Recent findings suggest that sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, speaks with reporters after votes in the Senate at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., Nov. 9, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images).

Sources indicate that "And, by the way, John Cornyn would have lost. It was just a point in time. John Cornyn would have lost by a lot. You know, one of those things. But he was beaten in the primary. And he's. He feels badly about it," the president continued.

"He's a nice guy, John Cornyn, but he's doing a tremendous disservice because Gaiser is fantastic.".

Cornyn wrote on X later Saturday, "If President Trump wanted to fill a judicial vacancy in Dallas, why did he wait until after the midterms to nominate someone?

"The seat has been vacant since 2025. Then, without any consultation, he nominates a non-Texan with little connection to the Lone Star State, with no trial court experience and who has not been appropriately vetted for a lifetime job. The Senate has a constitutional responsibility to provide 'advice and consent,' which is impossible without consultation," Cornyn added.

In a recent development, "Still, I would like to work with the President to fill the seat while we still have a Senate majority. I have forwarded an outstanding candidate who was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee, and who has now been interviewed by White House Counsel.

"All that is needed is an FBI background check (which) they stand ready to do on a timely basis," Cornyn also stated. "Back to you, Mr. President. Time is of the essence.".

Industry observers note that CORNYN MEETS WITH SEN-ELECT TALARICO, DESCRIBES HIM AS 'BASICALLY ... A GOOD PERSON'.

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called Cornyn's move "really frustrating," describing to Fox News' "Saturday in America" a tense encounter he had with Cornyn this week in Washington.

It has been revealed that "I came to him on the Senate floor, and I asked him to please let this judge go. And I tried to make the case on the merits that he'd make a fantastic judge. And I asked him, 'Will you just meet with him?' Because Cornyn refused even to meet with him," Cruz said.

"He wouldn't talk to him. He just stated, 'No, no, no.' And I was asking him, I said, 'Look, you're going to give this seat to the Democrats. Why would you want to do that?' And, unfortunately, he got very angry. He began screaming. He began cursing at me," Cruz added.

Cruz said, after the Republican losses in the midterm elections, "All the Republicans agreed, 'Let's do everything humanly possible to confirm every judge we can before the end of the year, because we know the Democrats are going to come in January,' and I expect they're going to block all judicial confirmations.".

TRUMP'S SUPREME COURT MAJORITY FACES LOOMING THREAT AFTER DEM SENATE TAKEOVER: 'STUCK'.

According to recent reports, assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser is interviewed in his office at the Department of Justice on Sept. 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Gaiser previously clerked for Supreme Court Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. (The Washington Post via Getty Images).

It has been revealed that "We had two vacancies in Texas, one in Austin that we're moving forward with. And we'll have that judge confirmed by the end of the year. We had a second vacancy in Dallas, and the problem was that we did not have time to have a brand-latest nominee go through the paperwork, the FBI background check," Cruz told Fox News.

According to recent reports, "That takes weeks and weeks and weeks, and we simply didn't have time between now and the end of the year to get that done. And, so, the White House proposed a different idea, which is to go with a senior lawyer at the Department of Justice, a man named Elliot Gaiser, an incredibly qualified judicial nominee.

"This is someone who was a law clerk at the U.S. Supreme Court for Justice Sam Alito. He was a state solicitor general arguing cases before the United States Supreme Court," Cruz said.

"And he's right now the head of the Office of Legal Counsel, which is the senior constitutional advisor to the president and the senior constitutional advisor to the attorney general.".

Cruz also told Fox News he interviewed Gaiser and called him "incredibly principled, smart, capable, ready.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in June 2026, Google and Voltus revealed a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM.
  • It has been revealed that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs.
  • Sources indicate that utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

According to recent reports, in June 2026, Google and Voltus revealed a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

It has been revealed that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

Utility programs and procurement.

Sources indicate that utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

Beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

Recent findings suggest that aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

Industry observers note that while Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

In a recent development, wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

Bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

The appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

According to recent reports, the biggest single media event of the decade took place on Thursday, and most of Washington missed it. Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest installment of the most popular video game series in the world, racked up nearly $1.5 billion in sales even before it introduced, already making back what may have been a more-than-a-billion dollar budget. In the next week, total sales are projected to hit over $3 billion. The previous game in the series still makes half a billion dollars a year through its online version alone. (For comparison purposes, Taylor Swift’s Eras tour, the biggest concert tour of all time, took in just over $2 billion, while Avengers: Endgame grossed roughly $2.9 billion.).

According to recent reports, video games are cultural juggernauts, and governments have noticed. Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest installment of the most popular video game series in the world, racked up nearly $1.5 billion in sales even before it introduced, already making back what may have been a more-than-a-billion dollar budget. Power Play: Video Games, Politics, and the Battle for Global Influence, George E. Osborn, Prometheus, 376 pp., July 2026, $34.95.

Video games are cultural juggernauts, and governments have noticed. As industry consultant George Osborn points out in his latest book, Power Play: Video Games, Politics, and the Battle for Global Influence, video gaming, once a solitary activity, has become a largely communal one. Online play creates a “third place” where people, especially the young, can mingle. As Osborn puts it, “what happens in video games communities bleeds out into reality—all the way into our political discourse.”.

Under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, for instance, Saudi Arabia has become a major force in video games, mostly through the power of capital. The prince, himself a keen gamer, is trying to encourage the creation of a domestic industry. He’s had little success so far, but Saudi money has succeeded in buying up existing companies, such as the giant Electronic Arts for $55 billion and the organization that created Pokémon Go for $3.5 billion.

Mohammed bin Salman wants to make money. But, as Osborn points out, he also wants to get gullible or greedy Westerners to help whitewash his corrupt, misogynistic autocracy. Buying gaming companies may be a more expensive route than donating to D.C. think tanks, but also perhaps a more effective one. Some industry insiders have already flagged worries about Saudi censorship in their games.

Sources indicate that an artist rendering of “The Line” in an undated image. NEOM.

But if the Saudi government is shaping video games, the influence is going the other way as well. Consider some of the crown prince’s grandiose projects. His proposal for The Line, a 106-mile-long and 650-foot-wide city, appeared to be inspired by the futuristic cities that appear in games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Deus Ex. The difference, of course, was that in reality The Line project was suspended after only 1.5 miles of foundation were dug.

It has been revealed that that feedback loop between gaming and reality is also evident when looking at another of Osborn’s case studies, Russia. Especially since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian studios have churned out propaganda games such as Squad 22: ZOV, which Osborn describes as an “objectively bad video game” but also a hub for anti-Ukrainian memes and a gathering place for ultranationalists.

Recent findings suggest that the fantasies of Russian games hook back into wider influence efforts. With the help of influencers such as streamer GrishaPutin, these games aim to boost morale and recruitment while also luring in foreign fighters, roughly 11,000 of whom have died fighting on the Russian side. Australian Daryl Fladung has been missing, believed dead, for several months after being recruited to come and fight for Russia (and post propaganda videos) through online war games. His last videos show him terrified and in pain.

Australian Daryl Fladung (right) and two fellow Russia-supporting British nationals on arrival in Moscow in an undated photo. Telegram: Ben Stimson.

In a recent development, russia’s reactionary politics are also attractive to some gamers. The gender split in gaming is roughly equal nowadays but the third place of popular games has a habit of becoming dominated by the loudest young men. It’s not uncommon for female players to conceal their gender, or even use a voice changer, to avoid harassment.

According to recent reports, that too has bled back into politics. Video game writers are generally liberal progressives, and there was a big push toward broadening representation in games in the 2010s, with female protagonists and people of color becoming more normalized. This was welcomed by many gamers but prompted a reactionary fury from others. The movement that resulted was Gamergate, which became part of the far-right’s attempt to woo younger male voters, with the encouragement of Steve Bannon. While it may have helped tip elections toward Donald Trump, it failed to produce any good games of its own.

Sources indicate that despite being the biggest video game market in the world, compared to Moscow, Beijing is far more reluctant to throw its weight around in gaming propaganda overseas. That’s in part because of a puritan communist dislike of any form of fun, leading to repeated crackdowns on minors playing games online and long delays before new games are officially approved.

Censorship at home is massive but, as Osborn notes, “Chinese games businesses invested billions of dollars in games businesses across the world to soften the blows landing on them from the CCP.” (pg. 151). Apart from some policing around Hong Kong and Taiwanese representation in games, those investments have mostly remained business-focused rather than trying to impose political limits. As with much else, China’s focus has been domestic control first, and foreign influence second.

The Honor of Kings International Championship in Shenzhen, China, on Dec. 3, 2022. Honor of Kings, a multiplayer online battle arena game, is operated by Tencent, China’s largest video game publisher.Honor of Kings/Tencent.

Sources indicate that but perhaps gaming’s biggest global influence lies in its role driving the AI industry, a story Osborn doesn’t cover in depth because much of it is so recent. Gaming depends on video cards, which are built with the high-end chips that also fuel the AI revolution. In fiscal year 2018, for instance, Nvidia made roughly 57 percent of its income from gaming. Last year, that figure was 7 percent, with roughly 90 percent coming from AI data centers.

It has been revealed that osborn highlights the role gaming played in driving forward the innovation needed for newer and better technology, especially in chip design. But the shift of the industry toward AI has left gamers deeply angry at Nvidia, a organization they once adored. (As a result, some of the best investigative reporting on Jensen Huang’s fall and Nvidia’s role in evading U.S. sanctions on China has come out of the games media.) Gaming hardware used to be getting cheaper and cheaper; the same setup would be half the price two years later. Thanks to the AI race, the reverse is now true. The gaming PC I bought for $1,600 the week Trump was elected for a second time, anticipating tariff rises, now retails at $2,600. It might seem a little silly to care deeply about your toys getting more expensive. But the contestation between gamers and AI companies is a microcosm of a wider concern: Who controls technological power?

Screen captures of the survival horror game Resident Evil Requiem, released in February, showing Nvidia’s upcoming graphics rendering model DLSS 5. It uses AI to infuse pixels with photorealistic lighting and materials. NVIDIA.

Personal computers have been the domain of tinkerers and inventors since they were first introduced at home. Now Sam Altman has put forward, then rapidly retracted, the idea that having RAM sitting in your own PC is “terrible” because it should be used by mega-corporations instead. In this context, the growing revolt against AI in video games—with players boycotting games that use AI art, AI writing, or even AI code—feels like part of something bigger.

Sources indicate that osborn’s final chapters are dedicated to promoting games that educate citizens and support the fight for democracy worldwide, from pro-Ukrainian stories to “green game jams” to promote climate awareness. But as long as the industry, and the technology that powers it, is in the hands of autocrats and tech tycoons, these aren’t the games we’ll be playing.

#111050. The Only Way to End the Netanyahu Era

The Only Way to End the Netanyahu Era

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026.
  • Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.
  • As the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026. He is the former leader of the Joint List and the Hadash party.

Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.

As the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament. The parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition command a clear majority in the Knesset, with 67 of its 120 seats. Yet the four Jewish-led parties in Eisenkot’s camp hold just 48 seats, leaving them unable to form a government on their own. The impasse echoes the prolonged political deadlock between 2019 and 2021, when Netanyahu’s supporters and his opponents remained locked in competing parliamentary blocs, and four consecutive elections failed to produce a stable governing majority.

But one thing is different this time. Israel’s Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Raam, are stronger than ever. Powered by extraordinary turnout among Arab citizens of Israel, they won a record 19 seats in the Knesset: 11 for the Joint List and eight for Raam. This political mobilization is important in itself, demonstrating Arab voters’ overwhelming desire for change and their recognition of the importance of participating in elections. But its significance goes far beyond the number of seats they have won. Together, the Arab parties now have the potential to be a decisive force in an anti-Netanyahu coalition, providing the parliamentary backing needed to form a government. The proof of this power has already been shown: on November 17, Arab support was crucial in the vote to replace the Likud speaker of the Knesset with a speaker from Eisenkot’s party. Now they have a historic opportunity to put the country on a different path.

As the first and former leader of the Joint List, I know how much is at stake. In 2019, I helped lead a groundbreaking effort to give Arab-led parties a direct voice in the Israeli political system. We took an enormous political risk by endorsing Benny Gantz, then a former chief of staff of the Israeli military and Netanyahu’s principal rival, as a candidate to form a government. We did so despite our profound political and ideological differences with him. Although that effort ultimately fell short, with Gantz choosing to pursue a “unity government” with Netanyahu instead, it established an vital precedent: by showing a willingness to work with Jewish political forces with whom they had deep disagreements, parties representing the Arab public had a real chance to prevent a Netanyahu-led far-right government from holding power.

According to recent reports, today, after nearly four years of disastrous leadership by Netanyahu and his far-right allies, that possibility has become far more urgent. It will take political courage on both sides. Eisenkot must be able to offer something to the Arab-led parties, and the Arab-led parties will need to be comfortable offering support to a government that they may not agree with on many concerns. But the remarkable Arab turnout and the sizable Israeli majority that is now against Netanyahu have pointed to a way forward. Not only Israel’s future but also its place in the region and the world may depend on the willingness of its leaders to engage with the country’s Palestinian minority. Ultimately, such a partnership will be essential to building the trust between Jews and Arabs that is a prerequisite to achieving any real progress toward a viable Israeli-Palestinian peace. This is the real choice now facing Israel: whether Israelis are prepared to replace the politics of supremacy and exclusion with a politics of equality.

Recent findings suggest that the factors that drove record numbers of Palestinian citizens of Israel to the polls in October have been years in the making. Although the country’s Arab citizens make up more than 20 percent of the Israeli electorate and have long made vital contributions to Israeli society as doctors, lawyers, engineers, high-tech professionals, and in many other fields, the Israeli right has for decades demonized them as enemies: a fifth column and a threat to the state. In recent years, this hostility has increasingly manifested itself in harassment and open racism at universities and workplaces, in the media, in the parliament, and in everyday life.

Yet it would be a mistake to assume that Arab exclusion has been driven only by Netanyahu and the radical right. Zionist parties of the center and the left have also contributed, by keeping a distance from Arab voters or simply ignoring them. The belief that Jewish citizens should ultimately determine the country’s political direction while Arab citizens must remain within whatever limits have been set for them runs deep in Israeli politics. Netanyahu understood early on how to turn this contradiction into a political strategy. Since the 1990s, he has repeatedly used the same formula: inciting his supporters against Arab citizens, delegitimizing Arab representatives in parliament, and convincing Jewish Israelis that a government that relies on Arab political support would somehow be illegitimate.

These tactics proved to be among Netanyahu’s most effective political tools, especially given that Arab-led parties have long been some of his biggest foes. He didn’t need to convince everyone to support his Likud party or its various coalition partners. He only needed to convince enough people, including Jewish Israelis who opposed him, that working with Arab-led parties was dangerous and unacceptable. Netanyahu’s strategy also helped suppress Arab turnout. Since the Arab-led parties had little chance of changing the status quo, Arab voters had little incentive to vote: for many years, a significantly lower proportion of Arab citizens went to the polls than did their Jewish counterparts.

In a recent development, that began to change in 2015 with the creation of the Joint List, which for the first time brought together four parties representing the Arab public on a single electoral ticket and which became the third-largest faction in the Knesset. By embracing a broader vision for our society, grounded in Jewish-Arab solidarity and opposition to the racism of the right, the Joint List demonstrated that Palestinian citizens of Israel could play a new and more influential role in the country’s political system. Then, under my leadership in 2019, the Joint List decided to back Gantz’s bid to unseat Netanyahu. The decision was highly controversial, both within the Arab electorate and across Israeli society. Many Arab voters were deeply ambivalent about supporting a potential government led by a former army chief whose political positions, particularly on the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the occupation, differed sharply from their own. Nevertheless, we were prepared to take that political risk because we understood that defeating Netanyahu was more vital.

In a recent development, in practice, our willingness to cooperate with the Zionist opposition was not, in fact, reciprocated. The Jewish opposition parties wanted our votes but could not bring themselves to accept us as equal political partners. And, ultimately, Gantz decided to form a government with Netanyahu instead. Nevertheless, the experience indicated that Jewish-Arab political cooperation could open up newly introduced horizons for a large segment of the public. Since then, every time that Arab-led parties have recommended or supported the effort of a Jewish candidate to form a government, or whenever the Israeli center-left has depended on their support, additional segments of Israeli society have become more open to this kind of cooperation.

It has been revealed that in 2021–22, an Arab party, Raam, joined the short-lived government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. I had serious reservations about the model of partnership that emerged, which seemed to rest on the expectation that Arab political representatives would limit their involvement to civilian and domestic matters, while refraining from addressing political and national questions, particularly the occupation and the Palestinian issue. I reject this distinction. We are part of the Palestinian people, and our identity and political concerns cannot be separated from our citizenship in Israel.

Recent findings suggest that but these kinds of slow and painful steps are how political change often happens in national struggles. It does not always begin with a moral or democratic awakening. Sometimes, it begins with pragmatic necessity. When there is no other option, people begin to reconsider what had once been seen as impossible. In the current election, that dynamic has become even more important. After the unending crisis of the past four years, many Israeli voters, including both Arabs and Jews as well as the leaders of most of the Zionist opposition parties, have concluded that getting rid of the Netanyahu government is more necessary than ever.

Recent findings suggest that in recent past elections, voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel has generally remained between 50 and 60 percent. What explains the unprecedented 20-percentage-point surge in turnout in the October election? Three developments stand out: the war of annihilation in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinians; the daily racism and hostility that Arab citizens now face in the streets, in public spaces, and in virtually every aspect of their lives; and the crime that has spiraled out of control in Arab communities under the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose policies have allowed it to flourish, and the relentless settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank enabled by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. All the grief and frustration accumulated over these years were brought to the ballot box.

Industry observers note that but there was another crucial factor as well. In the run-up to the election, Arab citizens, following the nearly even polls between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, could see in black and white just how much the outcome would depend on them. Voting this time would be more than a political choice. It was for many a personal responsibility and a way of taking control of their own future. That is why hundreds of thousands of Palestinian citizens of Israel made their way to the polls, defying years of efforts to silence them and undermine their political agency. Many understood that the future direction of the country might be quite literally in their hands.

I saw elderly people, like my friend Jumah from Jisr al-Zarqa, taking to the streets and campaigning for the Joint List. Many of them had lived through the 1948 nakba, or “catastrophe,” which accompanied Israel’s establishment and involved terrible massacres, the destruction of hundreds of Palestinian villages and towns, and the displacement of around 750,000 Palestinians. I saw young people debating politics in the cafes and restaurants of my beloved Haifa, persuading their friends to vote. I saw women and men from Nazareth, Umm al-Fahm, Sakhnin, Rahat, Akko, Kafr Yasif, Majd al-Krum, and countless other towns and villages united by a shared sense of purpose. I saw political consciousness become a living, collective force. For a moment, the boundaries between generations and communities seemed to disappear.

According to recent reports, the result marks a remarkable advance of the process of Arab participation in the Israeli political system that began in 2019. In this election, Arab citizens of Israel turned out in record numbers, dramatically narrowing the historical turnout gap with Jewish voters. And that has made another political reality increasingly clear: Israel’s liberal and centrist camp cannot form a government without the parties that represent the Arab public. If it excludes them, as well as the ultra-Orthodox and the far right, it will not reach the 61 seats needed. This is the demographic reality. Israeli Jews who oppose Netanyahu must decide whom they are willing to build a political future with.

According to recent reports, the debate about what Eisenkot should do and whether he should ask for Arab support is now unfolding beyond the Knesset, in people’s homes, cafés, in universities, and on the street. It is a deeply controversial question, and many Israelis disagree strenuously about it. Yet for the Arab-led parties, gaining sufficient importance to be able to provoke these conversations is an achievement. The fact that this debate is even taking place shows how the political process has caused Israelis to consider possibilities that until recently seemed unimaginable.

In the end, Eisenkot may have few other options if he wants to replace Netanyahu, as he has promised. In most cases, political parties support coalitions to advance positive changes and achieve concrete goals. But there are moments when political cooperation is necessary for a different reason: to prevent something far worse. The most immediate and overriding objective today is to bring an end to the far-right Netanyahu government. That is a priority on which both the Zionist opposition and the Arab-led parties can agree.

Beyond this shared basic goal, the Arab-led parties should use their political influence to work on two levels. First, they must seek tangible improvements in their constituents’ lives: combating organized crime in Arab communities, securing budgets, addressing the housing crisis, ending the brutal treatment of Palestinians living under occupation in the West Bank, and pushing for a permanent cease-fire and the reconstruction of Gaza. These are fundamental complications of human dignity and civilian life. On a broader level, they should continue to push for real progress on Israeli-Palestinian peace that is ultimately based on two states coexisting, side by side.

I do not expect the current Israeli political establishment to embrace these positions, but that does not mean that the Arab parties should not raise them at every opportunity. At the same time, the Arab parties can use their newfound political clout to build alliances between Jews and Arabs around shared political and strategic goals. The resulting partnerships must be about more than parliamentary arrangements; it must also create the foundations for a different future. That will require Jewish and Arab citizens of Israel to engage with one another on the basis of equality, rather than mere political convenience.

Thus far, Eisenkot has given few indications that he is prepared to go down this path. Since the election, it has been encouraging to see him condemn Netanyahu for fueling what he described as a “racist and violent” campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens. Yet many of the mainstream Zionist parties in Eisenkot’s camp have vowed not to work with the Arab parties. Still, Eisenkot must consider what that would mean. Thirty years from now, people will ask how Jewish supremacy became so normalized that even politicians who called themselves democrats accepted the exclusion of one-fifth of their fellow citizens. They will ask why Israel’s opposition could recognize the danger posed by Netanyahu’s government but not confront the assumptions that made his politics possible.

In a recent development, there is an irony in the fact that, in a country that seeks to keep political hegemony exclusively in Jewish hands, the Palestinian minority, after decades of struggle for political recognition and equal rights, has emerged as one of the most significant forces shaping the country’s political future. We have come to understand that we must be courageous and cooperate with the Zionist parties of the center and left in order to oust Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich. The question now is: Do these parties, which call themselves democratic and liberal, have the same courage?

Avoiding Colombia’s Escalation Trap

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.
  • How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones.
  • Recent findings suggest that on September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.

How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones.

Recent findings suggest that on September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta. Within hours, militants from that organization introduced a dramatic campaign of terror. The group, known colloquially as Los Pachenca, demanded that businesses across the city shutter. Some 90 percent of shops did, as videos circulated of gunmen shooting up storefronts that stayed open.

According to recent reports, for two decades, Los Pachenca has been the unquestioned criminal authority in the beachfront city and the adjacent Sierra Nevada mountain range, charging extortion payments from businesses and residents and controlling the flow of drugs out of the Port of Santa Marta, en route to Europe and beyond. But the level of control the group exhibited during the strike was particularly jarring, given that Santa Marta is the vacation home of many of the country’s elite and a common destination for international visitors. Colombia’s government responded by militarizing the city, sending in hundreds of soldiers and police officers, who rolled into town on the main highway with tanks and air support. Many shops still stayed closed until the morning of September 25, when the group confirmed that it was ending the strike. For locals, Los Pachenca’s reaction was a message about who remains in charge.

According to recent reports, calm has since returned to Santa Marta, but the incident may be indicative of risks to come. Colombia’s newly elected president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has promised a steep military escalation against illegal groups, which have grown precipitously in recent years. As he does so, armed and criminal organizations will undoubtedly respond. Often, their target will not be the state. Instead, they will likely direct their violence against the civilian populations, whom they have spent years coopting and coercing. That is because armed and criminal groups across the country have learned that their true leverage is their ability to govern local communities—and to intimidate and punish them into silence. Even when they do attack state forces, their use of weapons such as improvised explosives and makeshift drones means that bystanders often suffer. In one recent incident in the Pacific coast department of Valle del Cauca, four drone attacks released by an armed group in a single day left five civilians injured.

According to recent reports, these dangers are particularly acute as de la Espriella’s pledge of a zero-tolerance crackdown against armed and criminal groups has won enthusiastic support from Washington. Both countries want substantial and visible victories against these outfits. They triumphantly announced a newly introduced era of cooperation when the president took office in August, including a promise of upgraded military ties. (The United States has not yet publicly pledged new weapons, but it is already providing greater intelligence and logistical assistance on some operations.) After two years of tensions and threats between President Donald Trump and leftist former President Gustavo Petro, the political realignment means that Colombia is once again the United States’ closest defense ally in South America. This is likely to continue, despite major Democratic wins in the U.S. Congress, as the relationship’s focus on security has a long history of bipartisan support.

Industry observers note that this week, during U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Bogotá, the de la Espriella administration signaled that it would seek congressional approval for joint military operations with the United States in Colombia. This cooperation will likely yield initial results. The Colombian government has noted that it aims to ramp up attacks against armed and criminal groups and to go after leaders who enjoyed protection as counterparts in peace talks during the past administration.

In a recent development, yet Colombia’s true challenge is not how to carry out attacks but what to do afterward. Surgical strikes, which see the military enter and exit quickly, leave civilians more vulnerable in the aftermath, as armed groups retaliate against alleged informants and tighten their grip in areas they control. Bogotá must ensure that every operation includes contingencies to anticipate criminal groups’ reactions and build on successful offensives by weakening their grasp on communities. The government will need to strengthen the police’s ability to patrol contested areas, a costly but necessary process that the United States and other partners should support.

The stakes are high. Bogotá has a chance to leverage its increased military pressure to open the door for the state, rewriting the story of who governs conflict areas. If the government misses this opportunity to consolidate state control, however, Colombia risks entering an escalatory spiral in which civilians pay a mounting price for a campaign intended to protect them.

Armed and criminal groups have spent the last decade expanding their reach across Colombia. According to the local think tank Pares, the number of municipalities with an armed group presence rose from 212 in 2018 to 518 last year—or about half of all municipalities. This deterioration reversed dramatic and hard-won improvements in security. After the historically violent decades of the 1990s and 2000s, military pressure and negotiations yielded a 2016 peace agreement demobilizing the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), once the country’s dominant rebel group. Colombia’s countryside breathed a sigh of relief as the FARC pulled out of areas where it had been in control, which represented a quarter of the country’s land.

The FARC’s exit, however, did not pave the way for Colombia’s highly centralized and bureaucratic state to claim control of those vast geographies. Instead, old armed groups such as the National Liberation Army and newer ones such as the Gaitanista Army of Colombia (also known as the Gulf Clan) saw a chance to expand their access to trafficking routes, coca crops, illegal mines, and, ultimately, vulnerable rural populations. Kidnapping for extortion and mass displacement began to resurface, shattering optimism that progress would move in one direction. Over the last four years, membership in illegal groups has nearly doubled, to some 27,000 fighters today.

It has been revealed that as a candidate, de la Espriella successfully harnessed public frustration by promising mano dura, or iron-fisted tactics, including aerial attacks and increased incarceration, facilitated by the construction of mega-prisons. He blamed his predecessor’s administration for accelerating insecurity. The first leftist to be elected president in modern Colombia, Petro had entered office in 2022 vowing to de-emphasize the military’s role and instead hold peace talks with various armed organizations. But not every group participated, and many of the ones that did sought to take advantage of cease-fires to cement their control over communities. Midway through his term, Petro pivoted back toward deploying the armed forces. But much of the harm was already done.

Recent findings suggest that colombia’s upcoming president has been in office only a little more than 100 days, but the shift is marked. De la Espriella carried out three bombing raids in his first weeks. He has extradited dozens of individuals to the United States, including senior leaders, and the administration has killed or captured many others. The president is doggedly pushing to restart aerial fumigation of coca crops, which the state carried out in the early 2000s to try to reduce the number of hectares under cultivation; the practice has since been heavily restricted by court rulings over concerns about health and environmental consequences. Both in private and in public, military leaders laud the government’s new support for their operations.

Industry observers note that the Trump administration has also welcomed these developments, which align with a regional trend favoring Washington’s approach on counternarcotics. For Colombia, the newly introduced era of security cooperation with the United States represents a return to the status quo ante of the last quarter century, which was briefly disrupted by the Petro administration. U.S.-Colombian military ties were forged through antidrug efforts and deepened in 1999 with Strategy Colombia, a decadelong $10 billion aid package that funded, among other things, the expansion and professionalization of the security forces and fumigation. The Colombian police and military are deeply integrated with their American counterparts. They use U.S.- and NATO-compatible systems, travel by the hundreds to the United States each year for instruction, and receive American intelligence. In nearly every operation, at least one step (and often far more) in the logistical chain is either coordinated with Washington or relies on U.S. support. That relationship never fully stopped under Petro, but the two sides were notably wary of each other. Now bilateral trust appears to be restored.

Even before the elections, de la Espriella impressed U.S. officials by outlining his aims to reclaim security momentum for the state. The Colombian president is now acting on several explicit U.S. priorities, including extraditions and legislation to designate numerous groups as terrorist organizations. Meanwhile, Bogotá’s coca eradication targets are even more ambitious than Washington’s. At a personal level, relations are strong, too. Two of Colombia’s top military officials previously served as envoys to U.S. Southern Command.

According to recent reports, bogotá says that it intends to deliver results for Washington’s antidrug goals and has explicitly asked for additional support in the form of funding, aircraft, surveillance technologies, and maintenance. Although Colombia’s military remains among the best trained in the region, its logistical needs are critical. Only 13 of Colombia’s 53 Black Hawk helicopters are in working order, and defense spending has shrunk as a share of the national government’s budget, from 22.4 percent in 2003 to just 14.7 percent in 2025, with a growing proportion of those funds spent on salaries and pensions.

How much the United States will provide remains to be seen. In August, U.S. Southern Command’s General Francis Donovan discussed ways to shore up the deteriorating air fleet during a visit to Bogotá. The United States has also redeployed surveillance drones from Africa to Colombia and Ecuador, where they are already aiding intelligence collection. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio was reluctant to pledge specific aid while in Colombia in September, and most of this assistance is likely to be in kind or to stay in the hands of the U.S. military and contractors, with little entering the Colombian budget. Much of it appears to be focused on short-term offensive wins.

Industry observers note that colombia has returned to tactics such as aerial bombardment because they arguably worked against the FARC. Founded as a Marxist rebellion in the 1960s, the group behaved like a conventional army, dressed in uniforms, and sought out combat with the state. This meant that the Colombian military could bomb encampments and that capturing leaders left the organization at times rudderless. Slowly chipping away at the FARC’s hierarchy and control helped push the group to finally negotiate its disarmament, beginning in 2012.

It has been revealed that but today, those same strategies are yielding diminishing returns. The current generation of armed and criminal groups has little interest in confronting the state. Instead, they behave like businesses, seeking to safeguard access to natural resources, supply chains, and trafficking routes. They live within the civilian population and rarely wear uniforms. Leaders are easily replaced and hierarchies are fluid. Critically, Colombia’s armed groups have learned that wars with the military are costly but that controlling local populations—through intimidation and violence, but also by offering economic incentives, jobs, and services—is comparatively cheap. The battlefield has evolved from a conventional conflict to a contest over who can govern territories and the people living there.

Santa Marta offers an example of how this new model of warfare works. On most days, an outsider in the city would never perceive the presence of Los Pachenca. The group’s members do not patrol or identify themselves. Yet residents know them well from the weekly or monthly extortion payments they are forced to make. Local companies and government officials essentially view the group as an inescapable reality. Pushing back carries a violent price, but paying a protection tax, taking a bribe, or facilitating illegal commerce keeps business running smoothly.

In a recent development, the criminal governance of rural areas is even more suffocating. Groups that emerged from splinters of the former FARC, known as dissidents, often force local residents to hold identity cards, issued so that militants have a full census of who lives in the area and can detect possible enemy fighters. In the Amazon region, these groups keep a land registry more complete than that of the state so that they know exactly whom and how much to extort.

With this intense surveillance over society, armed and criminal groups frequently deploy the civilian population as human shields against military offensives and police patrols. The most egregious example is the widespread use of forcibly recruited children as bodyguards for senior commanders. De la Espriella’s initial bombardments, which killed at least six children, were even temporarily halted by a court over concerns about minors. Senior officers admit that these types of casualties are inevitable around high-value targets, and that the groups know that the military is far less likely to proceed if it means killing children.

In a recent development, armed and criminal groups will also try to use the military operations to their political advantage. When children are killed in bombardments, for example, FARC dissidents spin the local narrative into a story about how the state cares little for rural populations. The argument sticks because there is rarely a credible state presence that can serve and protect these same communities and earn their trust.

There are more immediate consequences, as well. In the aftermath of bombardments and high-level captures, armed and criminal groups often undertake what amounts to a purge of the population, killing or exiling anyone they believe to have collaborated with the state. And when the state takes out a leader, intra-group violence frequently ensues as former associates compete to take his place. Many residents shelter inside to avoid being caught up in the fighting, leaving children without school and parents without income. If fresh splinter groups emerge, the combat for control over neighborhoods can place even more civilians in the crossfire. This fallout widens the gap between immediate tactical results and long-term security gains. Taking out a senior leader wins applause, but conditions may well worsen on the ground.

De la Espriella’s administration has rightly identified winning territorial control, permanently dislodging criminal groups, and restoring state governance as its ultimate goals. The dilemma it now faces—exacerbated by U.S. support that focuses on attention-grabbing wins—is how to both achieve short-term results and ensure that these do not unleash fresh waves of violence, retaliation against civilians, and, in turn, criminal consolidation.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge is twofold. First, the military needs to anticipate groups’ violent reactions and to safeguard the population. In the case of Santa Marta, for example, the government could have increased police presence in the city in the hours after El Cholo was killed. Before the next bombardment or high-level capture, the state should ensure that a ground team of soldiers or military police is ready to hold the ground, protect the community, and prevent the armed group from swiftly stepping back in to reclaim territory.

The second challenge—establishing lasting territorial control—is trickier. A permanent rural security presence might offer the best chance for Colombia’s government to change the direction of the conflict. The country’s military leadership controls only the tip of the spear, not the rest of the state. Time and again, governments “send only the military to the hardest areas,” a retired senior officer told Crisis Group. Moreover, soldiers are operating under heavy pressure for quick wins, which are measured in the number of combatants and especially high-value targets that are killed or captured. There is a real risk that by focusing largely on these statistics, the state will overlook more comprehensive policies necessary to achieve durable security.

Sources indicate that pressure to deliver fast results has in the past incentivized unacceptable practices. In the early 2000s, intense political demands for combat kills fueled elaborate schemes in which soldiers murdered thousands of civilians and counted them as guerrilla fatalities, a scandal known as “false positives.” These crimes deeply compromised public trust in the security forces, and the military has worked for years to build a culture and procedures that ensure they do not happen again. Today, the country’s senior military leadership is likely the first and best brake on any attempts to use excessive force. Commanders say that they are cognizant of the need to guard against rules being slowly stretched until they are broken. “We need a stronger security approach, but it also worries us when we hear there is pressure for ‘results,’” one officer stated. But U.S. rhetoric and behavior, including its decision to sink what it claims are drug-smuggling boats on the high seas, compound these risks.

Success, then, may demand a strategy that is ultimately anchored in a much stronger and larger police force, fit for the job of safeguarding civilians rather than merely carrying out offensive strikes. Military operations can generate a window of opportunity by shuffling dynamics on the ground or removing certain dangerous players. Yet those reconfigurations will turn out in the state’s favor only if the resulting vacuum is eventually filled by reliable law enforcement. Take, for example, an operation that temporarily dislodges a group from a rural hamlet. If the military acts alone, it will likely enter and leave in a matter of days or even hours, allowing the armed group to promptly return. If, however, the offensive is followed up with permanent police patrols, access to the justice system, and social interventions, criminals will have a harder time regaining control.

This, of course, is easier mentioned than done, given the government’s resource constraints. To create effective and permanent patrols, police departments operating in the countryside need more officers and equipment to maintain a presence in the most remote communities. Colombia has roughly 180,000 uniformed police officers, a figure that, per capita, puts it on the lower end of OECD countries, many of which are far more urbanized and therefore easier to patrol. In Colombia’s conflict-affected areas, outgunned officers must often stay inside their local stations for their own safety, limiting their ability to build trust and channels of communication with the population. Other state institutions, such as the justice system, say that they cannot establish a durable foothold in villages without guarantees of protection in the medium term—exactly what rural policing should strive to provide. The U.S. State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs has funded the building and equipping of rural police stations in the past; it should expand this work. International partners with long-standing expertise in rural policing, such as Canada and France, could provide critical support, as well.

It has been revealed that in cities, the challenge is different. In Santa Marta, for example, the state is present, but it is weak and vulnerable to the pressure and cooptation of the same groups that it must confront. The police need both more officers and better working conditions—including salaries, benefits, access to education, and social support for families—that could help them resist bribes. Regular vetting and counterintelligence checks can help ensure that police are fighting on the side of the state and not its adversaries.

In a recent development, expanding the police will be an expensive, long-term undertaking. In the interim, Colombia could prioritize more personnel for critical areas and ensure that officers have a strong grounding in community policing, allowing them to understand the most pressing risks facing civilians. That means regular outreach to communities to build trust and make certain that officers are seen as having a stake in local well-being. The United States, meanwhile, must continue to help Bogotá strengthen its police and courts with direct financial and technical assistance.

It has been revealed that colombia, backed by renewed U.S. support, cannot afford to repeat past mistakes or ignore how the conflict has changed. Bogotá must therefore initiative for and capitalize on military pressure to do something no government in Colombia’s history has done: govern well in conflict areas.
